The Work and Torah Teaching of Mahari Bruna: A Comprehensive Historical and Halakhic Study of His Figure and Influence at the End of the Middle Ages
This composition surveys the life and Torah teaching of Mahari Bruna, one of the great halakhic decisors of Ashkenaz in the fifteenth century, who served as a halakhic bridge between the age of the Rishonim and the world of the Acharonim. The text describes how the rabbi coped with a stormy historical reality of persecutions, political imprisonments, and a famous blood libel in Regensburg, while establishing his standing as a revered spiritual leader. A central focus of the text is devoted to the responsa of Mahari Bruna, which serve as a historical source of great value for everyday Jewish life and constitute a decisive halakhic foundation for the rulings of the Rema in the Shulchan Arukh. The aim of the article is to present his figure as a critical link in the chain of transmission, which shaped Ashkenazic custom and halakha for generations.
The Work and Torah Teaching of Mahari Bruna: A Comprehensive Historical and Halakhic Study of His Figure and Influence at the End of the Middle Ages
The figure of Rabbi Israel ben Chaim Bruna, known as Mahari Bruna (c. 1400–1480), is one of the most central and fascinating junctions in the history of Ashkenazic Jewry in the fifteenth century.[1] This period, characterized by the transition between the authority of the "Rishonim" and the crystallization of the world of halakhic decision-making of the "Acharonim," was marked by political upheavals, bloody religious persecutions, and deep internal changes within the Jewish communal structure.[2] Mahari Bruna, as the foremost disciple of the great figures of the previous generation and as a decisor who passed on the foundations of halakha to the Rema, stands as a living bridge connecting the ancient Ashkenazic tradition with the modern era.[3] His work is not confined only to the four cubits of halakha; he was a public leader who contended with blood libels, imperial imprisonments, and fierce internal disputes, while preserving the world of Torah and the continuity of Ashkenazic custom under conditions of constant instability.[1, 4, 5]
Ashkenaz in the Fifteenth Century: The Historical and Spiritual Background of the Period
The fifteenth century in Germany and Central Europe was a period of gradual decline of the traditional Jewish center in the West and the strengthening of the new center in the East, mainly in Poland.[2] After the waves of pogroms of the fourteenth century, and especially after the Black Death (1348–1350), the Jewish communities in Ashkenaz were in a state of rehabilitation under heavy political and economic pressure.[6] The Holy Roman Empire, under the rule of Frederick III, regarded the Jews as "servants of the treasury" (Servi Camerae), which led to a policy of aggressive economic exploitation and the imprisonment of spiritual leaders as a means of pressure for collecting taxes.[4, 7]
Spiritually, the generation that preceded Mahari Bruna was led by figures such as the Maharil (Rabbi Jacob Moelln), who was regarded as the "father of Ashkenazic customs."[8] The Maharil worked to establish and fix prayer and custom, out of an understanding that dispersion and persecution threatened the unity of the tradition. Mahari Bruna grew up within this world, drawing from the teaching of those who continued the path of the Maharil, such as Mahari Weil and Rabbi Israel Isserlein.[2, 4] Understanding the geographical map of his life is essential for understanding his teaching.
Table of Geographical Transitions and Central Stations in the Life of Mahari Bruna
Biography and Wanderings: From the Community in Brno to the Rabbinate of Regensburg
Rabbi Israel was born in Brno (known in the Torah literature as "Bruna"), a central city in the region of Moravia in the Kingdom of Bohemia.[1] Already in his youth he stood out as a prodigy and as one who devoted himself "with all his body and soul" to the study of the Talmud.[1] He studied with the great sages of Ashkenaz of his generation: Rabbi David of Schweidnitz, Rabbi Zalman Cohen of Nuremberg, and above all with the two pillars of halakhic decision-making at that time – Rabbi Jacob Weil (Mahari Weil) and Rabbi Israel Isserlein (author of "Terumat HaDeshen").[4] These teachers not only imparted halakhic knowledge to him, but also ordained him to the rabbinate and expressed immense esteem for his abilities.[5, 9]
After his years of study he returned to his native city Brno and served there as rabbi.[1] However, his stability in the city was cut short in 1454, when the Jews of Brno were expelled from the city following a decree of King Ladislaus.[1, 7] This expulsion was part of a broader trend of dispossessing Jews from royal cities in Central Europe. Mahari Bruna moved to Prague for a short time, but ultimately found his place in the city of Regensburg (Ratisbon) in Bavaria.[5] Regensburg was at that time one of the most important and ancient communities in Germany, but Mahari Bruna's arrival in the city was not welcomed by the entire local leadership, which led to one of the most famous and painful rabbinic disputes of that century.[1, 4]
His Teachers and Their Influence on the Formation of His Torah Personality
Mahari Bruna's personality was shaped in the crucible of the Ashkenazic yeshivot that arose after the persecutions of the fourteenth century. His foremost teacher, Mahari Weil, was regarded as the central decisor of German Jewry in his generation, and his responsa and rulings on matters of ritual slaughter and inspection became inalienable assets ("iron-flock property").[1] Mahari Bruna saw himself as continuing the path of Mahari Weil in preserving the fine points of halakha and the customs of the communities.[5] Another decisive influence came from Rabbi Israel Isserlein, who was active in Wiener Neustadt. The halakhic dialogue between Mahari Bruna and Rabbi Israel Isserlein reflects deep mutual respect; Isserlein defended Bruna's authority in his later disputes and recognized him as a supreme Torah authority.[4, 9]
The combination of the deep learning of the Ashkenazic yeshivot with the practical need to answer the public's questions produced in Mahari Bruna a distinctive style of halakhic decision-making. He was not content with citing sources, but strove to understand the social and economic mechanisms of his time.[10] His teachers instilled in him the conception that the rabbi is not only a teacher of rulings, but a guardian of the community's walls, a role that at times requires standing firm against threats from within and without.[1]
The Dispute in Regensburg: A Struggle over Torah Territory and Rabbinic Ethics
When Mahari Bruna settled in Regensburg in 1456, he opened a yeshiva there and began to serve as a spiritual authority for a group of disciples and devotees.[4, 5] This move aroused the wrath of the rabbi of the local community, Rabbi Anschel Segal, who saw in it a violation of his rights and authority (trespass).[9] The dispute quickly intensified; the supporters of R. Anschel took humiliating measures against Mahari Bruna: they wrote the word "min" (heretic, "apikoros") on his seat in the synagogue, and when he rose to deliver a discourse, they organized a mass walkout of the congregation in order to shame him publicly.[1, 7]
Mahari Bruna displayed exceptional humility in the face of these attacks and chose not to fight back personally.[7] He turned to his teachers, Mahari Weil and Rabbi Israel Isserlein, to decide the issue. They ruled in his favor (see, for example, ruling 128 in Terumat HaDeshen), and determined that he had full right to teach and to serve in office in Regensburg.[4] The dispute subsided only with the death of Rabbi Anschel Segal, whereupon Mahari Bruna was accepted by all parts of the community as av beit din (head of the rabbinic court) and as the undisputed leader.[5, 7] This episode is studied to this day as a lesson in rabbinic ethics and in the balance of power within spiritual leadership.[7]
The Blood Libel of 1474: A Case Study of Religious Persecution in the Late Middle Ages
One of the most dramatic events in the life of Mahari Bruna, which became a symbol of the suffering of the Jews of Ashkenaz, is the blood libel in Regensburg in 1474.[4] The incident began when a convert from Judaism named Hans Vogl (or Vayol) accused Mahari Bruna, who was then about 74 years old, of purchasing a Christian child and murdering him in order to use his blood for baking matzot for Passover.[4, 7] This accusation, known as a "blood libel," was very widespread in Europe at that time and served as a tool for the dehumanization of Jews and often led to mass pogroms.[6, 11]
Bishop Henry and other Church officials hastened to declare Mahari Bruna guilty and demanded his execution.[7] Here, however, the political interests of the period intervened. The leaders of the city of Regensburg feared the wrath of Emperor Frederick III, who needed Mahari Bruna as an authority for the purpose of collecting taxes from the Jewish community.[7] In order to protect him from the incited mob while preserving the proceedings of "justice," he was imprisoned in the jail.[7] The Jewish community appealed for help to Emperor Frederick III and to King Ladislaus II of Bohemia, and both declared the rabbi's innocence, since blood libels had already been officially refuted by the papacy and the empire in the past.[1, 7]
In order to end the affair without provoking a popular uprising, the city authorities decided to put the accuser, Hans Vogl, to the test.[7] On the famous stone bridge of Regensburg, facing the executioner with a drawn axe, Vogl was required to confess his lie. Under threat of death he broke down and confessed that he had fabricated the accusation out of his hatred for the Jews and for the rabbi.[7] Vogl was sentenced to death by burning, and Mahari Bruna was released after 13 days of imprisonment, on the condition that he waive any claim for compensation for the imprisonment and the injustice done to him.[4, 7, 9]
Comparing the Regensburg Blood Libel with Similar Cases in the Fifteenth Century
The Rabbi as an Imperial Subject: Imprisonments and the Politics of Taxation
Beyond the blood libel, Mahari Bruna found himself at the center of political conflicts between the empire and the dukes of Bavaria. In 1456, shortly after his arrival in Regensburg, the rabbi was imprisoned for 13 days by order of Emperor Frederick III.[4] The reason for the imprisonment was the emperor's desire to force the Jewish community to pay the heavy "Coronation Tax."[4] The emperor understood that the key to collecting the funds passed through the spiritual leadership, since without the rabbi's instruction, members of the community might refuse or delay payment.[7]
The conflict was even more complex: the emperor regarded the Jews as his personal property, while Duke Ludwig of Landsberg also claimed rights over the Jewish taxes in the region.[1, 7] Mahari Bruna served, against his will, as a political pawn. His imprisonment was intended to pressure the community to hand over a considerable portion of its property (at times up to a third) to the imperial treasury.[2] This activity of Mahari Bruna in the area of communal taxation is well reflected in his halakhic responsa, which deal with the just distribution of the tax burden and the duty of obedience to the authorities in monetary matters.[10]
The Questions and Answers of Mahari Bruna: A Literary and Halakhic Analysis
The principal legacy of Mahari Bruna for the generations is the collection of his halakhic responsa, "Responsa of Mahari Bruna."[5] These responsa were collected and published after his death, and they constitute one of the most important sources for understanding the world of the sages of Ashkenaz in the fifteenth century.[10] Unlike earlier codes, the responsa present halakha as it is applied in practice in situations of crisis and of everyday life alike.[12]
Mahari Bruna's style in his responsa is characterized by deep Talmudic analysis that is nevertheless focused on a practical goal.[10] He combines immense erudition in the literature of the Rishonim with a sharp understanding of social reality.[4] Questions were addressed to him from throughout Central Europe, which attests that he was the "last decisor" of his generation after the death of Mahari Weil and Rabbi Israel Isserlein.[4]
Central Issues Appearing in the Responsa of Mahari Bruna
Distribution of taxes and property assessments (responsa 341–346): Mahari Bruna discusses in detail the internal mechanisms that the community should use to distribute the burden imposed by the authorities, while preserving distributive justice between rich and poor.[10]
The status of apostates and penitents (responsum 198): in light of the large number of apostates in his time (some of them under coercion), he addresses the proper halakhic attitude toward one who seeks to return to the rock from which he was hewn.[10]
Disguising Jewish identity (responsum 197): a fascinating question dealing with the possibility of Jews disguising themselves or concealing their identity in order to pass through countries where residence was entirely forbidden to them – living testimony to the dangers of the roads at that time.[10]
Leisure activities and society (responsum 71): a discussion of the question whether Jews are permitted to participate in or watch horse races, which shows the degree of Jewish involvement in the gentile social life of their surroundings.[10]
The Connection to the Rema and the Shaping of Halakha for the Generations
Mahari Bruna's historical importance grew in the sixteenth century, when Rabbi Moses Isserles (the Rema) wrote his glosses on the Shulchan Arukh, "the Mappah" (the Tablecloth).[1, 3] The Rema regarded Mahari Bruna as one of the three pillars of late Ashkenazic halakhic decision-making, alongside the Maharil and Rabbi Israel Isserlein.[3] Whereas Rabbi Yosef Karo relied mainly on the sages of Sepharad, the Rema used the responsa of Mahari Bruna as a primary source for determining custom and halakha for the Jews of Ashkenaz.[1, 5]
In almost every section of the Shulchan Arukh in which a gloss of the Rema appears noting "and some say..." or "and so they have practiced...," there is a high likelihood that the source for the matter is found in the writings of Mahari Bruna.[1, 3] This presence ensures that the voice of the rabbi of the Regensburg community continues to resonate and to influence the Jewish way of life to this very day.[5] This is a process of "canonization" of late Ashkenazic halakhic decision-making, in which Mahari Bruna serves as a critical link in the chain of transmission.[13]
The Historical and Sociological Material in the Responsa of Mahari Bruna
Modern scholars, among them Abraham Fuchs, have emphasized the immense historical value embodied in the responsa of Mahari Bruna.[13] The responsa are not merely a legal document; they provide glimpses into the personal lives, the dress, the language, and the material culture of the Jews of Germany in the fifteenth century.[10, 12] In his responsa one can find information on:
The attitude to oaths and waivers: how people sought to be rid of debts or obligations given in times of distress.[14]
The status of women and agunot: the decisor dealt with many cases of women left without their husbands as a result of frequent divorces and pogroms, and sought creative and bold ways to release them from their bonds.[10]
The structure of the synagogue: the dispute over the seat in the synagogue in Regensburg teaches of the social importance and status attached to seating places in the community.[1, 7]
The responsa also at times preserve nuances of the early Judeo-German language and legal concepts of the local German law, as they are reflected in the eyes of the rabbi.[10, 12] In this, Mahari Bruna acts as an unintentional historian, documenting the pulse of life of his people.[12]
His Legacy for the Generations and Textual Aspects of His Writings
The fate of the book of responsa of Mahari Bruna reflects the difficulties to which the Ashkenazic tradition was subject. The book was not printed during the author's lifetime, but only hundreds of years later.[4] The first edition was published in Salonika in 1788, but it was corrupt and full of many printing errors.[4] Another edition was printed in Stettin in 1860, but it too suffered from similar defects.[4, 9] Only in the modern era (the Jerusalem edition of 5720 and onward) was an academic and Torah effort made to produce a corrected edition based on manuscripts.[4]
The son of Mahari Bruna continued his path and served as a judge in Prague, a city that became the successor Torah center of the German communities that had disintegrated.[4] The fact that the disciples of Mahari Bruna, such as R. Zalman of Shutigwera (author of the book of the customs of the Maharil), continued to cite him and to rely on his rulings attests that his influence extended far beyond his local community.[2]
Summary and Conclusions: The Figure of Mahari Bruna in Historical Perspective
An examination of the work and teaching of Mahari Bruna reveals a multifaceted leader: a bold decisor, a devoted head of a yeshiva, and a statesman against his will.[1, 5] He succeeded in preserving the flame of Torah in one of the darkest periods of Ashkenazic Jewry, standing in the face of false accusations and internal wars.[2, 7]
His Torah teaching, as reflected in his responsa, constitutes an unassailable foundation for the Ashkenazic halakha accepted to this day.[3] His ability to combine abstract Talmudic logic with the practical needs of a society under siege made him a guide for the generations.[10, 12] Through the citations of the Rema, the rulings of Mahari Bruna became part of the DNA of modern Orthodox Judaism.[1]
The story of his rescue from the blood libel in Regensburg remains a testimony to the power of truth in the face of hatred, and to the importance of spiritual leadership that knows how to maneuver between the demands of the authorities and the needs of the community.[7] Mahari Bruna is not merely a figure from the past; he represents Jewish resilience and the ability to turn crisis and persecution into eternal halakhic creation.[5]
